Field surveys of the Round-scaled barbel (Barbus cyclolepis) in Bulgarian lowland rivers have documented that females attain sexual maturity upon reaching a total length of approximately 9 cm [Lp = approximately 9 cm], a threshold consistently observed across multiple sampling years. This length at puberty corresponds to a wet body mass of roughly 7.1 grams [Wwp = roughly 7.1 grams], indicating that females divert substantial somatic resources toward gonadal development once they cross this size boundary. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached a mean value of 11% [GSI = 11%] under laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At this temperature, the initiation of vitellogenesis and subsequent oocyte maturation proceed in synchrony, allowing gravid individuals to produce clutches of yolky, demersal eggs that adhere to submerged gravel substrates.

Newly hatched prolarvae of Barbus cyclolepis emerge from the chorion with a minute wet weight of only 0.0035 grams [Wwb = 0.0035 grams], a mass that reflects the relatively small egg diameter of approximately 1.9 mm typical of this species. These lecithotrophic larvae remain entirely dependent on their yolk reserves for the first several days, undergoing rapid absorption of endogenous nutrients before the mouth gapes fully and the onset of exogenous feeding begins. The transition to active prey capture represents a critical bottleneck, as the tiny yolk-sac fry must locate suitable zooplanktonic prey within the interstitial spaces of gravel beds or among marginal aquatic vegetation to avoid starvation. Despite their diminutive starting mass, the larvae exhibit a relatively fast growth trajectory during the first growing season, a pattern common among barbel species that exploit productive riverine habitats. The initial body size at eclosion imposes strong selection on early feeding performance and predator avoidance, with mortality rates typically highest during the first few weeks after hatching. The ability to achieve a rapid increase in length and mass during this vulnerable larval stage is essential for recruiting into the juvenile population before the onset of winter flow reductions and lower water temperatures that slow metabolic and digestive processes considerably.

A comprehensive growth analysis of the Round-scaled barbel population from the Struma River revealed that the largest individuals captured during extensive electrofishing campaigns reached a maximum total length of 30 cm [Li = 30 cm], a value representing the asymptotic size for this species in the region. The corresponding ultimate wet weight for specimens of this length was calculated at 275.6 grams [Wwi = 275.6 grams], a body mass that is rarely surpassed even in the most productive stretches of the river. This maximum size is considerably smaller than that of its larger congener, Barbus barbus, reflecting a life-history strategy that favors earlier maturation and higher relative reproductive output over the attainment of a massive adult body size. The length-weight relationship derived from the sample conforms closely to a power function, with the exponent indicating positive allometric growth in the species. Older adults exhibit a noticeable thickening of the body profile, particularly in the abdominal region, which accommodates the development of the gonads during the spawning season. The attainment of this ultimate length typically requires several years of steady growth, with the annual increment diminishing markedly after the onset of sexual maturity as resources are increasingly allocated toward gamete production rather than somatic expansion.

Reproductive investment in Barbus cyclolepis is intimately tied to the thermal conditions of the spawning season, and the species displays a maximum documented lifespan of 6,570 days [am = 6,570 days] when maintained at a constant water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C] in controlled laboratory aquaria. This longevity, equivalent to approximately eighteen years [am = approximately eighteen years], is among the highest recorded for small-bodied European barbels and suggests a relatively slow rate of physiological aging under optimal thermal cond at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]itions. In natural riverine environments, however, most individuals do not attain this remarkable age due to predation pressure, habitat degradation, and the energetic costs of repeated spawning events over several consecutive seasons. The extended lifespan allows for multiple annual reproductive bouts, a strategy that enhances lifetime fecundity and buffers against the stochastic recruitment failures that characterize lotic systems with variable spring floods. Older, larger females contribute disproportionately to population recruitment, as they produce clutches with higher numbers of eggs and larger oocytes that yield more robust, well-provisioned yolk-sac larvae. The capacity for such extended reproductive tenure underscores the importance of conserving older age classes within exploited populations, as their removal would disproportionately reduce the reproductive potential and resilience of the stock.

Feeding ecology studies conducted during the spring and summer months indicate that Barbus cyclolepis is a benthic omnivore, consuming a diet dominated by aquatic insect larvae, small crustaceans, and detrital organic matter collected from the riverbed. The species' subterminal mouth and fleshy lips are well adapted for foraging among cobbles and gravel, allowing individuals to dislodge prey items hidden beneath stones. Comparisons with sympatric cyprinids reveal that the Round-scaled barbel occupies an intermediate trophic position, neither specializing entirely on invertebrates nor relying heavily on plant material, a flexibility that likely enhances its ability to persist in food webs subject to seasonal fluctuations in prey abundance. Growth increments during the juvenile stage are strongly influenced by local productivity, with individuals from nutrient-rich reaches below agricultural catchments achieving faster length gains than those from oligotrophic headwater streams. The species also exhibits a degree of trophic plasticity, with larger adults occasionally incorporating small fish and fish eggs into their diet when such resources become available during the spawning aggregations of other riverine fishes. This dietary breadth, combined with the life-history traits described above, reinforces the status of Barbus cyclolepis as a resilient, generalist inhabitant of the Balkan ichthyofauna, capable of adapting to moderate anthropogenic alterations in its riverine environment.
